drills.q: Name the 7 GoF structural patterns and group them into 'common in real backends' vs 'rare/situational.'
drills.a: Common: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy. Situational/rare: Composite (needs genuinely recursive domain data), Bridge (needs 2 independently-varying hierarchies), Flyweight (needs measured extreme object-count memory pressure).

drills.q: Distinguish Adapter, Facade, Decorator, and Proxy along two axes: does the interface change, and is new behavior added?
drills.a: Adapter: interface changes, no new behavior (compatibility). Facade: many interfaces simplify to one, no new behavior (simplicity). Decorator: interface stays the same, adds stackable behavior (extension). Proxy: interface stays the same, controls access, sometimes adds behavior like caching (control).

drills.q: A vendor payment SDK is called directly from 200 call sites and the vendor just deprecated a method. What should have been in place, and what's the fix now?
drills.a: An Adapter layer (a PaymentGateway interface with one vendor-specific implementation) should have confined vendor-specific code to one file. The fix now is a wide, mechanical, risky refactor to introduce that adapter retroactively -- exactly the cost the pattern exists to avoid paying later.

drills.q: Explain why decorator stacking order is not commutative, with a concrete logging+caching example.
drills.a: @logged over @cached (logged outermost) logs every call including cache hits, since logged wraps the whole cached call. @cached over @logged (cached outermost) means cache hits short-circuit before ever reaching the logger, so hits go unlogged. Outermost decorator always sees the call first and the return value last.

drills.q: Diagnose: an ORM-backed endpoint iterating 1000 orders and reading order.customer on each is making 1000 extra queries. What pattern is responsible and what's the fix?
drills.a: This is the classic N+1 failure mode of a lazy-loading Proxy: accessing the relation transparently triggers a fresh query per access instead of one batched query. Fix with explicit eager loading (joinedload/selectinload in SQLAlchemy, Preload in GORM, JOIN FETCH in JPQL) on the hot path.

drills.q: A Facade class has grown to 40 public methods, imports from 15 modules, and contains its own conditionals and state. What's wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: It has drifted from a thin delegation layer into a God Object wearing a Facade's name -- the tell is business logic living inside the facade instead of in the components it should delegate to. Fix: split along real subsystem boundaries (e.g. OrderFacade, RefundFacade, ReportingFacade) so each stays a pure composition of calls.

drills.q: When is Bridge actually justified versus being over-engineering, and how does it differ from Strategy?
drills.a: Bridge is justified only when there are 2 independent hierarchies (e.g. N shape types x M rendering backends) that would otherwise multiply into an NxM subclass explosion. If only one implementation exists on one side, plain DI with a single interface is enough. Structurally Bridge and Strategy are nearly identical (interface + swappable implementation); they differ only in intent -- Bridge prevents a hierarchy explosion, Strategy swaps one algorithm.

drills.q: Design the integration layer for a service supporting 3 LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, local vLLM) behind one internal call, and explain the limit of the pattern when providers have different capabilities.
drills.a: Define an LLMClient interface (generate(prompt, **kwargs) -> Response) with one Adapter per provider translating each SDK's distinct auth/streaming/usage-field shape into the common interface, confining provider-specific breaking changes to one file each. The limit: Adapter can't paper over genuine capability gaps (e.g. only one provider supports function calling) -- that needs an explicit capability-detection/registry layer rather than silently no-op'ing unsupported features inside the adapter.

drills.q: Why is Flyweight rarely hand-built in Python or the JVM, and when would you still build one?
drills.a: Both runtimes already deduplicate the common cases (Python's small-integer cache and string interning, the JVM's string pool and boxed-Integer cache), so a custom Flyweight adds redundant complexity for primitive-sized data. Build one only when profiling shows real, measured memory pressure from millions of larger near-duplicate domain objects (e.g. font glyphs, tokenizer vocab entries, game tile types) that the runtime isn't already sharing.
